    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}

   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}

   145	follows.

   148	definition of canonical linear map).

   155	$v$.

   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$

   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.

   465	\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
   466	The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
   467	as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
   468	sections.
   469	The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
   470	of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
   471	The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
   472	the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
   473	tuple $\ldparams$ as input.
   474	
   475	
   476	
   477	\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the classical low-degree test]
   478	  \label{lem:ld-complexity}
   479	  Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$ denote a parameter tuple.
   480	  \begin{enumerate}
   481		\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   482	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ is $\poly(m, d, k, \log q)$.
   483		\item The time complexity of evaluating marginals of the CL functions
   484	    $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$, and $L_\DLine$ at a given input point is $\poly(m, \log
   485	    q)$.
   486		\item The Turing machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   487	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ can be computed from $\ldparams$ in $\polylog
   488	    (q,m,d,k)$ time.
   489	  \end{enumerate}
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	
   492	\begin{proof}
   493		Finite field arithmetic over $\F_q$ can be performed in time $\polylog q$, by
   494	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   495		The most expensive step in $\decider^\ld$ is to evaluate a univariate
   496	  polynomial $f: \F_q \to \F_q^k$ at some point $t_u \in \F_q$ that corresponds
   497	  to a point $u \in \F_q^m$, which takes time $\poly(m,d,k,\log q)$.
   498	  The function $L_\Point$ is a projection onto $V_\xpt$, which takes time
   499	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ to compute (it just involves ``zeroing out'' the registers
   500	  outside of $V_\xpt$).
   501	  The functions $L_\ALine$ and $L_\DLine$ require computing a canonical linear
   502	  map, which requires performing Gaussian elimination and can be done in time
   503	  $\poly(m,\log q)$.
   504	
   505	  The Turing-machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ can be
   506	  uniformly computed from the integers $(q,m,d,k)$ expressed in binary; the
   507	  complexity of computing the description comes from describing the parameter
   508	  tuple $\ldparams$, which takes time that is at most polynomial in the bit
   509	  length of $(q,m,d,k)$.
   510	\end{proof}

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.

   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_A: \mH_A \to \mH_{A'} \otimes \mH_{A''},\phi_B: \mH_B \to \mH_{B'} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ (where $\mH_{A'},\mH_{B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mH_{A''},\mH_{B''}$ are finite dimensional) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{A''} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ such that 
   625	\begin{enumerate}
   626	    \item $\left \| \phi_A \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \ket{\aux} \right \| \leq O(\sqrt{\eps})$,
   627	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have that
   628	    \begin{gather*}
   629	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^X_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   630	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^Z_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   631	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^X_b)_{B'} \\
   632	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^Z_b)_{B'}
   633	    \end{gather*}
   634	    where the $\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}_{A'B'} \otimes \ket{\aux}_{A''B''}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$. As a consequence, letting 
   635	    \begin{gather*}
   636	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_1 \\
   637	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_1 \\
   638	    \end{gather*}
   639	    it holds that
   640	    \begin{gather*}

640	    \begin{gather*}
   641	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} \otimes I_{B' B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \otimes I_{B' B''} \\
   642	        I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \;,
   643	      \end{gather*}
   644	      where the notation $M \approx_{\delta} N$ for $M, N$ that are not POVM
   645	      elements means
   646	      \[  \bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi}  \leq  O(\delta). \]
   647	\end{enumerate}
   648	
   649	\end{theorem}
   650	\begin{proof}
   651	 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.
   652	\end{proof}
   653	
   654	We will need the following theorem,
   655	which shows that any pair of anticommuting observables 
   656	can be used to form a value-$1$ strategy for the Magic Square game.
   657	
   658	\begin{theorem}
   659	  \label{thm:ms-from-ac}
   660	  Let $A = \{A_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ and $B = \{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ be two-outcome
   661	  projective measurements acting on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n}$ which are consistent on
   662	  $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$, and let $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 - A_1$ and
   663	  $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ be the corresponding observables.
   664	  Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = -\mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A$.
   665	  Then there exists a symmetric strategy $\strategy = (\psi, M)$ for the Magic
   666	  Square game with the following properties.
   667	  \begin{enumerate}
   668	  \item $\strategy$ is an SPCC strategy of value $1$.
   669	  \item The state $\ket{\psi}$ has the form $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes
   670	      n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   671	  \item For $b \in \{0,1\}$, we have $M^{\Variable_1}_b = A_b \otimes I$ and
   672	    $M^{\Variable_5}_b = B_b \otimes I$.\label{item:embeds}
   673	  \end{enumerate}
   674	\end{theorem}
   675	
   676	\begin{proof}
   677	  The strategy~$\strategy$ is based on the canonical two-qubit strategy for the
   678	  Magic Square game as described in, for example,~\cite{aravind2002simple}.
   679	  The state is $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   680	  We specify the measurements of~$\strategy$ in
   681	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} as an \emph{operator solution} for the Magic
   682	  Square game, meant to be read as follows: each cell contains a two-outcome
   683	  projective measurement $\{E_0, E_1\}$ on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n} \otimes \C^2$
   684	  written as its \emph{$\pm 1$-valued observable} $E_0 - E_1$.
   685	  When Player~$\alice$ or~$\bob$ receives the question $\Variable_j$ for $j \in
   686	  \{1, \ldots, 9\}$, they measure their share of~$\ket{\psi}$ using the
   687	  measurement specified by the cell corresponding to~$\Variable_j$ and receive a
   688	  single-bit measurement.
   689	  When they receive the question $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,6\}$,
   690	  they simultaneously perform the three measurements in the corresponding row or
   691	  column on $\ket{\psi}$ to obtain three bits.
   692	  For example, if Player~$\alice$ receives question~$\Variable_1$, they
   693	  measure~$\ket{\psi}$ using the measurement $\{A_0 \otimes I, A_1 \otimes I\}$
   694	  corresponding to the observable $\cal{O}_A \otimes I$ (where the first
   695	  operator acts on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ and the second acts on
   696	  $\ket{\EPR_2}$).
   697	  Similarly, on question~$\Variable_5$, they use the measurement $\{B_0 \otimes
   698	  I, B_1 \otimes I\}$.
   699	  This establishes Item~\ref{item:embeds} of the theorem.

   723	  First, we show that this gives a well-defined strategy.
   724	  The $\Variable_j$ measurements are well-defined because each cell contains a
   725	  $\pm 1$-valued observable.
   726	  This is obvious for all $j \neq 9$; when $j = 9$, the bottom-right cell
   727	  contains $\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$.
   728	  Because~$\cal{O}_A$ and~$\cal{O}_B$ anti-commute,
   729	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:am-i-hermitian}
   730	  \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X
   731	  = - \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   732	  = \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   733	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^\dagger.
   734	  \end{equation}
   735	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian. In addition, 
   736	  \begin{equation*}
   737	  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^2
   738	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X) \cdot (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   739	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \cdot \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A) \otimes (\sigma^Z \sigma^X \cdot \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   740	  = I,
   741	  \end{equation*}
   742	  where the first step uses Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian} and the final
   743	  step uses the fact that $\cal{O}_A, \cal{O}_B, \sigma^X, \sigma^Z$ are $\pm
   744	  1$-valued observables and hence square to the identity.
   745	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian and squares to the identity.
   746	  Therefore, it is a $\pm 1$-valued observable.
   747	  
   748	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements,
   749	  we must show that the three measurements in each row and column are simultaneously measurable.
   750	  This is equivalent to the three $\pm 1$-valued observables being simultaneously diagonalizable,
   751	  which is equivalent to them being pairwise commuting. This can be easily verified for the cases of $i = 1, 2, 4, 5$
   752	  (i.e.\ the first two rows and columns).
   753	  In the case of $i = 3$, commutativity of $\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X$ 
   754	  follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}.
   755	  Since these two matrices commute, they also commute with their product 
   756	  $(\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z)(\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X) = \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$.
   757	  The case of $i = 6$ is similar.
   758	  
   759	  By construction, $\strategy$ is symmetric, and we have already shown that it
   760	  is projective.
   761	  It remains to show that it is commuting, consistent, and value~$1$.
   762	  To show that it is commuting, it suffices to show that the measurement for
   763	  each cell is simultaneously measurable with all three measurements in its row
   764	  or column, which was already proved above.
   765	  Now we show consistency of the measurements.
   766	  We will show this by instead showing consistency of their observables.
   767	  By this we mean the following: if $E = \{E_0, E_1\}$ is a two-outcome projective measurement on $\cal{H}$
   768	  then its corresponding $\pm 1$-valued observable $\cal{O} = E_0 - E_1$
   769	  is consistent on a state $\ket{\phi} \in \cal{H} \otimes \cal{H}$ if
   770	  \begin{equation*}
   771	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi} = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi}.
   772	  \end{equation*}
   773	  This is in fact equivalent to the notion of $E$ being consistent on $\ket{\phi}$ from Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement}.
   774	  To see this, if $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$, then so is $\cal{O}$, because
   775	  \begin{equation*}
   776	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   777	  = (E_0 - E_1) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   778	  = I_{\alice} \otimes (E_0 - E_1) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   779	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi},
   780	  \end{equation*}
   781	  where the second equality is by consistency of~$E$.
   782	  On the other hand, suppose $\cal{O}$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   783	  Then because $E_0 + E_1 = I$, we can write $E_0 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O})$ and $E_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I - \cal{O})$.
   784	  As a result,
   785	  \begin{equation*}
   786	  E_0 \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   787	  = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   788	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   789	  = I_{\alice} \otimes E_0 \cdot \ket{\phi},
   790	  \end{equation*}
   791	  and similarly for $E_0$. Thus, $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   792	  This proves the equivalence.
   793	  
   794	  Now we use this to prove consistency of $\strategy$.
   795	  To begin, we note that because $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ by assumption,
   796	  so to are their $\pm 1$-valued observables $\cal{O}_A$ and $\cal{O}_B$.
   797	  Next, we note that $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$;
   798	  to verify this, we recall that $\sigma^X \ket{0} = \ket{1}$ and $\sigma^X \ket{1} = \ket{0}$, and so
   799	  \begin{align*}
   800	  \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}
   801	&  =   \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{00} + \ket{11})\\
   802	&  = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{10} + \ket{01})
   803	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{11} + \ket{00})
   804	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}.
   805	  \end{align*}
   806	  This shows $\sigma^X$ is consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$,
   807	  and a similar argument shows the same for $\sigma^Z$.
   808	  We now use these two facts to show that the observable in each cell of
   809	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   810	  To see why, consider the $j = 9$ case:
   811	  \begin{align*}
   812	&  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\alice \otimes I_\bob
   813			\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2} \\
   814	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X)_\bob
   815	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^X$}\\
   816	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes I)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   817	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^Z$}\\
   818	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \otimes I)_\alice \otimes ( \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   819	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_B$}\\
   820	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   821	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_A$}\\
   822	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\bob
   823	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}. \tag{by Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}}
   824	  \end{align*}
   825	  The remaining cases of $j \in\{1, \ldots, 8\}$ are similar, and we omit them.
   826	  This shows that the observable in each cell is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$,
   827	  and as a result the corresponding two-outcome projective measurements are consistent as well.
   828	  As a result, the $\Variable_j$ measurements are consistent.
   829	  
   830	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements, each such measurement $\{F_{a, b,
   831	    c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$ is of the form $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b
   832	  \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   833	  But then consistency of~$F$ follows from the~$\Variable$ consistencies:
   834	  \begin{align*}
   835	  F_{a, b, c} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}
   836	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c)_{\alice} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\\
   837	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi} \tag{consistency of $E^3$}\\
   838	 &   = (E^1_a)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^2$}\\
   839	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^1_a)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^1$}\\
   840	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^2_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{commutativity of $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$}\\
   841	 &               = I_{\alice} \otimes F_{a, b,c} \ket{\psi}.
   842	  \end{align*}
   843	  Hence, all measurements are consistent.
   844	  
   845	  Since all measurements are consistent, this implies that the answer bit of the
   846	  player receiving a $\Variable$ question is always consistent with the
   847	  corresponding answer bit of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question.
   848	  Similarly, the answers of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question
   849	  always satisfy the given constraint; observe that in all rows and the first
   850	  two columns, the observables multiply to $I$, whereas the observables in the
   851	  last column multiply to $-I$.
   852	  This implies that the strategy is value-$1$.
   853	  To see why, 
   854	  let us again consider a $\Constraint_i$ measurement, which we write as $F=\{F_{a, b, c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$.
   855	  As above, it can be written as  $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   856	  Consider the measurement $S=\{S_0, S_1\}$ that corresponds to measuring $\{F_{a, b, c}\}$ and then outputting the sum of measured values of~$a$, $b$, and~$c$.
   857	  In other words,
   858	  \begin{equation*}
   859	  S_0 = F_{0, 0, 0} + F_{0, 1, 1} + F_{1, 0, 1} + F_{1, 1, 0},
   860	  \qquad
   861	  S_1 = F_{0, 0, 1} + F_{0, 1, 0} + F_{1, 0, 0} + F_{1, 1, 1}.
   862	  \end{equation*}
   863	  The following expression gives a convenient formula for the $\pm 1$-valued observable $S_0 - S_1$:
   864	  \begin{equation*}
   865	  (E_0^1 - E_1^1) \cdot (E_0^2 - E_1^2) \cdot (E_0^3 - E_1^3)
   866	  = E_0^1 E_0^2 E_0^3 - E_0^1 E_0^2 E_1^3 - E_0^1 E_1^2 E_0^3 + E_0^1 E_1^2 E_1^3 + \cdots
   867	  = S_0 - S_1.
   868	  \end{equation*}
   869	  When we are looking at $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$,
   870	  the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $I$, and so $I = S_0- S_1$.
   871	  Because $S_0$ and $S_1$ are both positive semidefinite,
   872	  this is true only if $S_0 = I$ and $S_1 = 0$, which implies that the three bits output by $F$ always sum to~$0$.
   873	  As a result, this strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_i$ question.
   874	  On the other hand, when $i = 6$, then the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $-I$,
   875	  and so $S_1 = I$, and the three bits sum to~$1$.
   876	  Thus, the strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_6$ question as well.
   877	  This concludes the proof.
   878	\end{proof}

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,

900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}

   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   926	\subsection{Linear spaces and registers}
   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).
   945	
   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}
   953	  We also write $\ket{\EPR}_{\F_q}$ as $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}$ as
   954	  $\ket{\EPR}$.
   955	\end{definition}

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations

  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates

  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}

   270	/-- Reuse an already chosen field model for successor parameters. Since Lean
   271	prefers larger numeric priorities, this transport uses `200` so it is tried
   272	before the canonical fallback above. -/
   273	instance (priority := 200) {params : Parameters} [inst : FieldModel params.q] :
   274	    FieldModel params.next.q := by
   275	  simpa [Parameters.next] using inst
   276	
   277	abbrev Scalar (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q] := FieldModel.K params.q
   278	abbrev PolynomialModel (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q] :=
   279	  MvPolynomial (Fin params.m) (Scalar params)
   280	abbrev LinePolynomialModel (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q] :=
   281	  _root_.Polynomial (Scalar params)
   282	
   283	/-- The chosen scalar model for the paper's `F_q` has exactly `q` elements
   284	(`preliminaries.tex`, lines 17--19 and 89--93). -/
   285	@[simp] theorem scalar_card (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q] :
   286	    Fintype.card (Scalar params) = params.q := by
   287	  simp [Scalar]
   288	
   289	/-- Interpret a coded coordinate in `Fin q` as a scalar in the chosen field model. -/
   290	def decodeScalar {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x : Fq params) : Scalar params :=
   291	  (FieldModel.equiv (q := params.q)).symm x
   292	
   293	/-- Re-encode a field-model scalar as its canonical representative in `Fin q`. -/
   294	def encodeScalar {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x : Scalar params) : Fq params :=
   295	  FieldModel.equiv (q := params.q) x
   296	
   297	@[simp] theorem encode_decodeScalar {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x : Fq params) :
   298	    encodeScalar (decodeScalar x) = x := by
   299	  simp [encodeScalar, decodeScalar]
   300	
   301	@[simp] theorem decode_encodeScalar {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   302	    (x : Scalar params) :
   303	    decodeScalar (encodeScalar x) = x := by
   304	  simp [encodeScalar, decodeScalar]
   305	
   306	/-- The zero coordinate. -/
   307	def zeroCoord {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] : Fq params :=
   308	  encodeScalar 0
   309	
   310	/-- Coordinate addition transported through the `Fin q` coding. -/
   311	def addCoord {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x y : Fq params) : Fq params :=
   312	  encodeScalar (decodeScalar x + decodeScalar y)
   313	
   314	/-- Coordinate subtraction transported through the `Fin q` coding. -/
   315	def subCoord {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x y : Fq params) : Fq params :=
   316	  encodeScalar (decodeScalar x - decodeScalar y)
   317	
   318	@[simp] theorem addCoord_subCoord_right {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   319	    (x y : Fq params) :
   320	    addCoord y (subCoord x y) = x := by
   321	  unfold addCoord subCoord
   322	  rw [decode_encodeScalar]
   323	  simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   324	
   325	@[simp] theorem addCoord_subCoord_left {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   326	    (x y : Fq params) :
   327	    addCoord (subCoord x y) y = x := by
   328	  unfold addCoord subCoord
   329	  rw [decode_encodeScalar]
   330	  simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   331	
   332	@[simp] theorem subCoord_addCoord_right {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
   333	    (x y : Fq params) :
   334	    subCoord (addCoord x y) y = x := by
   335	  unfold subCoord addCoord
   336	  rw [decode_encodeScalar]
   337	  simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   338	
   339	/-- Coordinate multiplication transported through the `Fin q` coding. -/
   340	def mulCoord {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x y : Fq params) : Fq params :=
   341	  encodeScalar (decodeScalar x * decodeScalar y)
   342	
   343	/-- Coordinate inversion transported through the `Fin q` coding. -/
   344	def invCoord {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (x : Fq params) : Fq params :=
   345	  encodeScalar ((decodeScalar x)⁻¹)
   346	
   347	/-- Pointwise addition in the coded ambient space. -/
   348	def addPoint {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (u v : Point params) : Point params :=
   349	  fun i => addCoord (u i) (v i)
   350	
   351	/-- Scalar multiplication in the coded ambient space. -/
   352	def smulPoint {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] (t : Fq params) (u : Point params) :
   353	    Point params :=
   354	  fun i => mulCoord t (u i)
   355	
   356	/-- The zero point in `F_q^m`. -/
   357	def zeroPoint {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q] : Point params :=
   358	  fun _ => zeroCoord
   359	
   360	/-- The inclusion of the first `m` coordinates into `m + 1` coordinates. -/
   361	def embedCoord (params : Parameters) : Fin params.m → Fin params.next.m :=
   362	  fun i => ⟨i.1, Nat.lt_trans i.2 (Nat.lt_succ_self params.m)⟩
   363	
   364	/-- The old-coordinate inclusion into the appended coordinate space is injective. -/
   365	theorem embedCoord_injective (params : Parameters) :
   366	    Function.Injective (embedCoord params) := by
   367	  intro i j hij
   368	  apply Fin.ext
   369	  simpa [embedCoord] using congrArg Fin.val hij
   370	
   371	/-- The last coordinate of `F_q^(m+1)`. -/
   372	def lastCoord (params : Parameters) : Fin params.next.m :=
   373	  ⟨params.m, Nat.lt_succ_self params.m⟩
   374	
   375	/-- No old coordinate is the appended last coordinate. -/
   376	theorem embedCoord_ne_lastCoord (params : Parameters) (i : Fin params.m) :
   377	    embedCoord params i ≠ lastCoord params := by
   378	  intro h
   379	  have hval := congrArg Fin.val h
   380	  simp [embedCoord, lastCoord] at hval

     3	/-!
     4	# Basic finite-dimensional matrix operators
     5	
     6	This module contains the elementary trace and matrix-algebra facts used by the
     7	finite-dimensional quantum layer.  It introduces the local operator abbreviation
     8	`Op d = Matrix d d ℂ` and keeps the basic trace bookkeeping independent of the
     9	positive-semidefinite order and normalized-trace material.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The declarations in this file are matrix facts for the LDT
    14	formalization of `references/ldt-paper/`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder Matrix.Norms.Elementwise
    18	open WithLp
    19	
    20	namespace Matrix
    21	
    22	/-! ### Trace bookkeeping -/
    23	
    24	/-- Reindexing rows and columns by the same equivalence preserves matrix trace.
    25	
    26	This generic matrix lemma is used when moving between equivalent finite index
    27	presentations of the same operator. -/
    28	theorem trace_reindex {α β R : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    29	    [AddCommMonoid R] (e : α ≃ β) (M : Matrix α α R) :
    30	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.reindex e e M) = Matrix.trace M := by
    31	  classical
    32	  simp only [Matrix.trace, Matrix.diag_apply, Matrix.reindex_apply]
    33	  rw [← e.symm.sum_comp (fun i : α => M i i)]
    34	  rfl
    35	
    36	/-! ### Linear matrix maps -/
    37	
    38	/-- Taking a submatrix is linear in the ambient matrix.
    39	
    40	This packages the entrywise linearity of `Matrix.submatrix` in the same style
    41	as Mathlib's block-diagonal additive and linear maps. -/
    42	def submatrixLinearMap (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    43	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    44	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) :
    45	    Matrix m n α →ₗ[R] Matrix m' n' α where
    46	  toFun := fun A => Matrix.submatrix A row col
    47	  map_add' := by
    48	    intro A B
    49	    ext i j
    50	    rfl
    51	  map_smul' := by
    52	    intro c A
    53	    ext i j
    54	    rfl
    55	
    56	@[simp]
    57	theorem submatrixLinearMap_apply (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    58	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    59	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) (A : Matrix m n α) :
    60	    Matrix.submatrixLinearMap R row col A = Matrix.submatrix A row col :=
    61	  rfl
    62	
    63	/-- The trace pairing of two block-diagonal matrices is the sum of the trace
    64	pairings of the corresponding diagonal blocks. -/
    65	theorem trace_blockDiagonal_mul {o m R : Type*}
    66	    [Fintype o] [DecidableEq o] [Fintype m] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring R]
    67	    (B D : o → Matrix m m R) :
    68	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.blockDiagonal B * Matrix.blockDiagonal D) =
    69	      ∑ b : o, Matrix.trace (B b * D b) := by
    70	  rw [← Matrix.blockDiagonal_mul B D, Matrix.trace_blockDiagonal]
    71	
    72	end Matrix
    73	
    74	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    75	
    76	/-! ### Basic operator type -/
    77	
    78	/-- Square complex matrices as the finite-dimensional operator algebra. -/
    79	abbrev Op (d : Type*) := Matrix d d ℂ
    80	
    81	/-! ### Kronecker product bookkeeping -/
    82	
    83	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the right factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    84	theorem kronecker_sub_right
    85	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A : Op d₁} {B₁ B₂ : Op d₂} :
    86	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂ =
    87	      Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    88	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) = -Matrix.kronecker A B₂ := by
    89	    simpa using (Matrix.kronecker_smul (-1 : ℂ) A B₂)
    90	  calc
    91	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂
    92	        = Matrix.kronecker A B₁ + Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) := by
    93	            rw [hneg]
    94	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
    95	    _ = Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    96	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.kronecker_add A B₁ (-B₂)).symm
    97	
    98	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the left factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    99	theorem kronecker_sub_left
   100	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A₁ A₂ : Op d₁} {B : Op d₂} :
   101	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B =
   102	      Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   103	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B = -Matrix.kronecker A₂ B := by
   104	    simpa using (Matrix.smul_kronecker (-1 : ℂ) A₂ B)
   105	  calc
   106	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B
   107	        = Matrix.kronecker A₁ B + Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B := by
   108	            rw [hneg]
   109	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   110	    _ = Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   111	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.add_kronecker A₁ (-A₂) B).symm
   112	
   113	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

     3	/-!
     4	# Matrix-valued measurements for the MIP*=RE project
     5	
     6	This file provides the matrix-valued measurement layer used by the LDT formalization.
     7	
     8	## Main definitions
     9	
    10	* `Submeasurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to at most the identity.
    11	* `Measurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to exactly the identity.
    12	* `Submeasurement.postprocess` — data-processed submeasurements via answer relabeling.
    13	* `Measurement.postprocess` — the paper's postprocessing proposition for complete POVMs.
    14	* `inconsistency` — the off-diagonal mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`.
    15	* `diagOverlap` — the diagonal mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`.
    16	
    17	## References
    18	
    19	This file builds the project's finite-dimensional measurement layer on top of
    20	the normalized-trace and positive-operator facts in `MIPStarRE.Quantum.FiniteMatrix`
    21	for the quantum formalization in `references/ldt-paper/`.
    22	-/
    23	
    24	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    25	
    26	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    27	
    28	/-! ## Submeasurements and measurements -/
    29	
    30	/--
    31	A submeasurement on a finite answer type `α` is a family of PSD matrices
    32	`M : α → Op d` with `∑ a, M a ≤ 1`.
    33	-/
    34	structure Submeasurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] where
    35	  /-- The effect operators. -/
    36	  effect : α → Op d
    37	  /-- Each effect is positive semidefinite. -/
    38	  pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a
    39	  /-- The effects sum to at most the identity. -/
    40	  sum_le_one : ∑ a, effect a ≤ 1
    41	
    42	/--
    43	A measurement is a submeasurement whose effects sum exactly to the identity.
    44	-/
    45	structure Measurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    46	    extends Submeasurement α d where
    47	  /-- The effects sum to the identity. -/
    48	  sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1
    49	
    50	/-! ## Totals and postprocessing -/
    51	
    52	namespace Submeasurement
    53	
    54	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    55	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    56	
    57	/-! ### Totals and postprocessing -/
    58	
    59	/-- The total operator `∑ a, M_a`. -/
    60	noncomputable def total (M : Submeasurement α d) : Op d :=
    61	  ∑ a, M.effect a
    62	
    63	/--
    64	Data processing: relabel the answer set by `f : α → β`, summing the effects over
    65	fibers.
    66	-/
    67	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    68	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) : Submeasurement β d where
    69	  effect b := ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    70	  pos b := Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => M.pos a
    71	  sum_le_one := by
    72	    calc
    73	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    74	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
    75	      _ ≤ 1 := M.sum_le_one
    76	
    77	/-- Restatement of `sum_le_one` in terms of the named total operator. -/
    78	theorem total_le_one (M : Submeasurement α d) :
    79	    M.total ≤ 1 := by
    80	  simpa [total] using M.sum_le_one
    81	
    82	/-- Postprocessing preserves the sum of all effects. -/
    83	theorem postprocess_sum_eq [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    84	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    85	    ∑ a, M.effect a = ∑ b, (M.postprocess f).effect b :=
    86	  (Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect).symm
    87	
    88	/-- Postprocessing preserves the named total operator. -/
    89	theorem postprocess_total [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    90	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    91	    (M.postprocess f).total = M.total := by
    92	  simpa [total] using (M.postprocess_sum_eq f).symm
    93	
    94	end Submeasurement
    95	
    96	namespace Measurement
    97	
    98	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    99	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
   100	
   101	/--
   102	Build a complete measurement from effects whose sum is exactly the identity.
   103	
   104	This constructor keeps the equality proof as the primary hypothesis and derives
   105	the inherited submeasurement inequality automatically.  It is useful at paper
   106	sites that are explicitly POVMs rather than relaxed sub-POVMs.
   107	-/
   108	def ofSumEqOne (effect : α → Op d) (pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a)
   109	    (sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1) : Measurement α d where
   110	  effect := effect
   111	  pos := pos
   112	  sum_le_one := le_of_eq sum_eq_one
   113	  sum_eq_one := sum_eq_one
   114	
   115	/-- The named total of a complete measurement is the identity. -/
   116	theorem total_eq_one (M : Measurement α d) :
   117	    M.total = 1 :=
   118	  M.sum_eq_one
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Postprocess a complete measurement by relabeling outcomes.
   122	
   123	This formalizes `references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex:169--180`: regrouping
   124	the effects along the fibers of `f` preserves the total operator, so a POVM
   125	remains a POVM after postprocessing.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   128	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) : Measurement β d where
   129	  toSubmeasurement := M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f
   130	  sum_eq_one := by
   131	    calc
   132	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
   133	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
   134	      _ = 1 := M.sum_eq_one
   135	
   136	@[simp] theorem postprocess_effect [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   137	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) (b : β) :
   138	    (M.postprocess f).effect b =
   139	      ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a :=
   140	  rfl
   141	
   142	@[simp] theorem postprocess_to_submeasurement [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   143	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) :
   144	    (M.postprocess f).toSubmeasurement = M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f :=
   145	  rfl
   146	
   147	end Measurement
   148	
   149	/-! ## Overlap definitions -/
   150	
   151	section Overlap
   152	
   153	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   154	variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   155	
   156	/-- The off-diagonal overlap mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`. -/
   157	noncomputable def inconsistency (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   158	  ∑ a, ∑ b ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun b => b ≠ a), normalizedTrace (M a * N b)
   159	
   160	/-- The diagonal overlap mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`. -/
   161	noncomputable def diagOverlap (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   162	  ∑ a, normalizedTrace (M a * N a)
   163	
   164	end Overlap
   165	
   166	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

     3	import Mathlib

     5	/-!
     6	# Distribution infrastructure for the low individual degree test
     7	
     8	Shared distribution definitions: finite-support weighted distributions,
     9	a probability predicate, push-forward distributions, weighted-sum linear maps,
    10	averaging, uniform distribution, and outcome summation.
    11	
    12	Note: this module contributes declarations to the comparator statement closure
    13	of `mainFormal`, which must elaborate in the same environment as the
    14	Mathlib-only `Challenge.lean`.  Keep the full `import Mathlib`; do not narrow
    15	it.  See `docs/comparator.md`, "Environment alignment".
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    21	
    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1
    38	
    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]

   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm
   117	
   118	namespace Distribution.IsProbability
   119	
   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   127	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   128	
   129	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   130	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   131	than over a stored support finset. -/
   132	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   133	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   134	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   135	  rw [Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support 𝒟 𝒟.weight 𝒟.outsideSupport]
   136	  exact h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   137	
   138	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   139	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   140	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   141	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   142	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   143	
   144	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   145	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   146	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   147	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   148	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   149	
   150	end Distribution.IsProbability

   152	namespace Distribution
   153	
   154	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   155	whose total mass is one.
   156	
   157	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by
   158	`ENNReal.ofReal`; the hypotheses of `PMF.ofFinset` are exactly the project
   159	probability invariant and the stored zero-off-support condition. -/
   160	noncomputable def toPMF {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   161	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) : PMF α :=
   162	  PMF.ofFinset (fun a => ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a)) 𝒟.support
   163	    (by
   164	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   165	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   166	      simp)
   167	    (by
   168	      intro a ha
   169	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   170	      simp)
   171	
   172	@[simp]
   173	theorem toPMF_apply {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   174	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   175	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a) := rfl
   176	
   177	@[simp]
   178	theorem toPMF_apply_toReal {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   179	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   180	    (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a).toReal = 𝒟.weight a := by
   181	  rw [toPMF_apply, ENNReal.toReal_ofReal (𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   182	
   183	/-- The associated PMF has zero mass outside the stored support of the project
   184	distribution. -/
   185	theorem toPMF_apply_of_notMem {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   186	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {a : α} (ha : a ∉ 𝒟.support) :
   187	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = 0 := by
   188	  rw [toPMF_apply, 𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   189	  simp
   190	
   191	/-- The project push-forward agrees with Mathlib's push-forward of the
   192	associated probability mass function. -/
   193	theorem toPMF_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   194	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   195	    (𝒟.map e).toPMF (h𝒟.map e) = (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟).map e := by
   196	  classical
   197	  ext b
   198	  rw [toPMF_apply, PMF.map_apply, map_weight]
   199	  rw [ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg
   200	    (s := 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b))
   201	    (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   202	  rw [tsum_eq_sum (s := 𝒟.support)]
   203	  · rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   204	    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   205	    intro a ha
   206	    by_cases hea : e a = b
   207	    · have hba : b = e a := hea.symm
   208	      rw [if_pos hea, if_pos hba, toPMF_apply]
   209	    · have hba : b ≠ e a := fun hba => hea hba.symm
   210	      rw [if_neg hea, if_neg hba]
   211	  · intro a ha
   212	    by_cases hba : b = e a
   213	    · rw [if_pos hba, toPMF_apply_of_notMem 𝒟 h𝒟 ha]
   214	    · rw [if_neg hba]
   215	
   216	end Distribution
