   173	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]\label{def:state-distance}
   174		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ be two families of states in the same space $\mathcal H$. For a function $\delta \colon \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted $\ket{\psi} \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if
   175		\[
   176			\lVert \ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n} \rVert^2 = O(\delta(n))\,.
   177		\]
   178		The dependence of the states and of $\delta$ on the indexing parameter $n$ is generally left implicit; we write, e.g., $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.
   179	\end{definition}
   180	
   181	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
   182		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   183		Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
   184		\[
   185			A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
   186		\]
   187		on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   188		\[
   189			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
   190		\]
   191		In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
   192	\end{definition}
   193	
   194	A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.
   195	
   196	% The source (references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:257-274) states this
   197	% definition for pairs of POVMs but applies the relation to arbitrary operator families:
   198	% to plain operators at 06:313-330, to sets of matrices at 06:364-380, and to products and
   199	% commutators, compared against the zero family, at 06:409-445. The general form below,
   200	% for arbitrary finite families of operators, is the one of the NEEXP source
   201	% (references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:385-391), from which the distance
   202	% calculus is imported; the POVM case is singled out after the display.
   203	\begin{definition}[State-dependent distance between operator families]\label{def:povm-distance}
   204		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   205		Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ and $\{N^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be two families of linear operators on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   206		\[
   207			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_a \lVert (M^x_a - N^x_a)\, \ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le O(\delta)\,,
   208		\]
   209		and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state $\ket{\psi}$ and the distribution $\mu$ are clear from context. This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance. The principal case is that in which $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are POVMs on $\mathcal H$, and we then speak of the state-dependent distance between the POVMs; but the relation is used for arbitrary operator families --- for instance for products of measurement operators, or for commutators compared against the identically zero family, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:commutation-analysis} below.
   210	\end{definition}
   211	
   212	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]\label{def:strategy-distance}
   213		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:state-distance, def:povm-distance}
   214		Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game and let $\mathcal S = (\psi, A, B)$ and $\mathcal S' = (\psi', A', B')$ be strategies for $\mathfrak G$. For $\delta \in [0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\mathcal S$ is $\delta$-close to $\mathcal S'$} if the following conditions hold.
   215		\begin{enumerate}
   216			\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   217			\item For all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $y \in \mathcal Y$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations holding under the distribution $\mu$ (i.e.\ under its corresponding marginals), on either $\ket{\psi}$ or $\ket{\psi'}$.
   218		\end{enumerate}
   219	\end{definition}
   220	
   221	\begin{remark}[Asymptotic reading of the distance relations]\label{rem:asymptotic-distance}
   222		Definitions~\ref{def:state-distance}, \ref{def:consistency}, and \ref{def:povm-distance} are asymptotic: every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement refers to families of states and measurement families indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and the $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n \to \infty$. None of these relations is a pointwise inequality with an explicit constant. By contrast, the corresponding relations used in the low individual degree chapters (Definitions~\ref{def:simeq} and~\ref{def:approx_delta}) carry no hidden constant. Any explicit quantitative version of the present relations therefore retains the constants absorbed into the $O(\cdot)$; for instance, the triangle inequality of Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle} carries a factor $2$ inside the $O(\cdot)$.
   223	\end{remark}

   227	\begin{lemma}[Consistency versus closeness; Facts 4.13 and 4.14 in \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\label{fact:agreement}
   228		\uses{def:consistency, def:povm-distance}
   229		For POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$, the following hold.
   230		\begin{enumerate}
   231			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
   232			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ \emph{and} $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are projective measurements, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
   233			\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ and either $\{A^x_a\}$ or $\{B^x_a\}$ is a projective measurement, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_{\delta^{1/2}} \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
   234		\end{enumerate}
   235	\end{lemma}
   236	\begin{proof}
   237		Stated in the source without proof; these are Facts 4.13 and 4.14 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. For the first item, expand each term $\lVert (A^x_a \ot \Id - \Id \ot B^x_a)\ket{\psi} \rVert^2$ and use $ (A^x_a)^2 \le A^x_a$, $(B^x_a)^2 \le B^x_a$ together with completeness of the two POVMs: summing over $a$ and averaging over $x$ bounds the total by at most twice the off-diagonal mass, which is $O(\delta)$ by hypothesis. When both families are projective the two operator inequalities hold with equality, so the expansion equals exactly twice the off-diagonal mass; reading this identity in the other direction gives the second item. For the third item, write the off-diagonal mass $\sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi}$ as an inner product involving $(A^x_a \ot \Id - \Id \ot B^x_a)\ket{\psi}$, using projectivity of one of the two families, and apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality; this route costs a square root in the error.
   238	\end{proof}

   240	\begin{lemma}[Fact 4.20 in \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\label{fact:add-a-proj}
   241		\uses{def:povm-distance}
   242		Let $\mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mathcal C$ be finite sets, and let $\mu$ be a distribution over question pairs $(x,y)$. Let $\{A^x_{a,\,b}\}$ and $\{B^x_{a,\,b}\}$ be operators whose outcomes range over the product set $\mathcal A \times \mathcal B$. Suppose a set of operators $\{C^y_{a,\,c}\}$, whose outcomes range over the product set $\mathcal A \times \mathcal C$, satisfies the condition $\sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \le \Id$ for all $a$ and all $y$. If $A^x_{a,\,b} \approx_\delta B^x_{a,\,b}$ on average over $x$ sampled from the corresponding marginal of the distribution $\mu$, then $C^y_{a,\,c} A^x_{a,\,b} \approx_\delta C^y_{a,\,c} B^x_{a,\,b}$ on average over $(x,y)$ sampled from $\mu$.
   243	\end{lemma}
   244	\begin{proof}
   245		Fix questions $x, y$ and answers $a \in \mathcal A$, $b \in \mathcal B$. Then
   246		\begin{align*}
   247			\sum_c \bigl\lVert (C^y_{a,\,c} A^x_{a,\,b} - C^y_{a,\,c} B^x_{a,\,b})\, \ket{\psi} \bigr\rVert^2
   248			&= \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b})^\dagger \Bigl( \sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \Bigr) (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b}) \ket{\psi}\\
   249			&\le \bigl\lVert (A^x_{a,\,b} - B^x_{a,\,b})\, \ket{\psi} \bigr\rVert^2\,,
   250		\end{align*}
   251		where the inequality uses the assumption $\sum_c (C^y_{a,\,c})^\dagger C^y_{a,\,c} \le \Id$. Summing over $a, b$ and averaging over $(x,y) \sim \mu$ yields the conclusion.
   252	\end{proof}

   254	\begin{lemma}[Multiplying by function-indexed operators]\label{fact:add-a-proj2}
   255		\uses{def:povm-distance}

   270	\begin{lemma}[Absorbing an approximating family into a projective sum]\label{lem:cool-closeness-fact}
   271		\uses{def:povm-distance, def:povm-conventions}
   272		Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$.    287		where the last step uses $A^x_a \le \Id$. All expectations are taken according to $\mu$, and the last quantity is $O(\delta)$ by the assumption $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$ (Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance}), which is the bound required for the conclusion.

   322	The state-dependent distance is the right tool for reasoning about the closeness of measurement operators in a strategy. The following lemma converts joint consistency with a single projective measurement into an approximate commutation relation.
   323	
   324	\begin{lemma}[Approximate commutation from joint consistency]\label{lem:commutation-analysis}
   325		\uses{def:povm-distance, def:povm-conventions}

   327		\begin{align*}
   328			A^x_{a,\,b} \ot \Id_B &\approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,b}\,,\\
   329			C^x_{a,\,c} \ot \Id_B &\approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\,,
   330		\end{align*}

   332		\[
   333			[A^x_{a,\,b},\, C^x_{a,\,c}] \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta 0\,.
   334		\]

   337		\uses{fact:add-a-proj, fact:triangle}

   339		\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   340			A^x_{a,\,b}\, C^x_{a,\,c} \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta A^x_{a,\,b} \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\,.
   341		\end{equation}

   343		\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutation-analysis-2}
   344			A^x_{a,\,b} \ot B^x_{a,\,c} \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,c}\, B^x_{a,\,b} = \Id_A \ot B^x_{a,\,b,\,c}\,.
   345		\end{equation}

   441	\section{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
   442	% Paper subsection label sec:cl kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   443	\label{sec:cl}
   444	
   445	Conditionally linear functions specify the question distributions of the games considered in the following chapters in a form that can be ``introspected''. Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element $x \in V = \F^n$ and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially to $x^{V_j}$, where $V_1, V_2, \dots$ is a sequence of complementary register subspaces such that both the linear map $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$, for $j \ge 2$, may depend on the values taken by the previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$, $L_2(x^{V_2})$, and so on.
   446	
   447	Throughout this section $V$ denotes the linear space $\F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$, and all the distinguished subspaces of $V$ are register subspaces (Definition~\ref{def:register-subspace}). If $V_1, V_2, \dots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, we use the subscript range notation
   448	\[
   449		V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j < k} V_j\,, \qquad V_{>k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,\ell \ge j > k} V_j\,,
   450	\]
   451	and $V_{\le k}$, $V_{\ge k}$ are understood to be $V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively. For a register subspace $V'$ of $V$, the symbol $x^{V'}$ denotes the projection of $x$ onto $V'$ parallel to the complementary register subspace (Definition~\ref{def:complementary}). Moreover, if $F \colon V' \to V'$ is a function and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ for $F(x^{V'})$; for example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is shorthand for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
   452	
   453	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear functions]\label{def:cl-func}
   454		\uses{def:register-subspace, def:complementary}
   455		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n \ge 0$. For all integers $\ell \ge 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined inductively as follows.
   456		\begin{enumerate}
   457			\item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the $0$ function on $V$.
   458			\item Let $\ell \ge 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear functions has been defined. The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form: there exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and, for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\,v}$ on $V_{>1}$, such that for all $x \in V$,
   459			\[
   460				L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})\,.
   461			\]
   462		\end{enumerate}
   463	\end{definition}
   464	
   465	We abbreviate ``conditionally linear'' as \emph{CL}. Operationally, an $\ell$-level CL function first applies $L_1$ to $x^{V_1}$; conditioned on the value $x^{L_1}$ it selects a register subspace $V_2$ and a linear map $L_2$ and applies $L_2$ to $x^{V_2}$; and so on, finally outputting $\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} x^{L_k}$. Every $1$-level CL function is linear, and conversely every linear map on $V$ is a $1$-level CL function. Moreover, for every $\ell \ge 1$ the collection of $\ell$-level CL functions contains the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level CL functions.
   466	
   467	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear distributions]\label{def:cl-dist}
   468		\uses{def:cl-func}
   469		Let $L, R \colon V \to V$ be conditionally linear functions. The \emph{conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ corresponding to $(L,R)$} is the distribution over pairs $(L(x), R(x)) \in V \times V$ for $x$ drawn uniformly at random from $V$.
   470	\end{definition}
   471	
   472	Note that both players' questions are generated from the \emph{same} uniformly random seed $x$; this shared-seed structure is what the introspection technique exploits. The following lemma elucidates the structural properties of $\ell$-level CL functions. Recall that $x^{L_{<k}}$ and $x^{L_k}$ denote $L_{<k}(x)$ and $L_{k,\,u}(x^{V_{k,\,u}})$ where $u = L_{<k}(x)$.
   473	
   474	\begin{lemma}[Structure of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-kth}
   475		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   476		Let $\ell \ge 1$ and $V = \F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$. A function $L \colon V \to V$ is an $\ell$-level CL function if and only if the following collection of functions and subspaces exists:
   477		\begin{enumerate}
   478			\item[(i)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, a function $L_{\le k} \colon V \to V$, called the \emph{$k$-th marginal of $L$};
   479			\item[(ii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a register subspace $V_{k,\,u}$ of $V$, called the \emph{$k$-th factor space with prefix $u$};
   480			\item[(iii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a linear map $L_{k,\,u} \colon V_{k,\,u} \to V_{k,\,u}$, called the \emph{$k$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$};
   481		\end{enumerate}
   482		such that the following conditions hold for all $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$:
   483		\begin{enumerate}
   484			\item $L_{\le k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$;
   485			\item $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell} V_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$ for all $x \in V$;
   486			\item $L_{\le k}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} x^{L_i}$ for all $x \in V$, where $L_i$ is shorthand notation for $L_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$;
   487			\item $L = L_{\le \ell}$.
   488		\end{enumerate}
   489		As in condition 3, we sometimes use $V_k$ and $L_k$ to denote $V_{k,\,u}$ and $L_{k,\,u}$ respectively, leaving the prefix $u$ implicit.
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	\begin{proof}
   492		\uses{def:cl-func}
   493		For the ``if'' direction, conditions 1 and 4 immediately exhibit $L$ as an $\ell$-level CL function. For the ``only if'' direction one constructs the marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps by induction on $\ell$. In the base case $\ell = 1$ take $L_{\le 1} = L$, $V_1 = V$, and $L_1 = L$. For the inductive step, write $L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})$ as in Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} and apply the inductive hypothesis to each $(\ell-1)$-level function $L_{>1,\,v}$, obtaining its marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps over $V_{>1}$. Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ with first factor space $V_1$, and for $k \ge 2$ define $L_{\le k}(x) = x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\,<k}(x^{V_{>1}})$, with the $k$-th factor space and linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$ given by those of $L_{>1,\,v}$ at index $k-1$ with prefix $w$, where $v = u^{V_1}$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}}$. Conditions 1--4 are then verified directly from the inductive hypothesis: the direct-sum decomposition of $V_{>1}$ extends to $V$ by adjoining $V_1$, and the sum formula for $L_{\le k}$ follows by unfolding the inductive marginals.
   494	\end{proof}
   495	
   496	The marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given CL function $L$ need not be unique. For example, the identity function on $V = \F^n$ is a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a $k$-level CL function for any $k \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition of $V$ into factor spaces.

   498	\begin{lemma}[Concatenation of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-concat}
   499		\uses{def:cl-func}
   500		Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and let $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces. Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and, for each $u \in L(U)$, $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL function on $V$. Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$, defined by
   501		\[
   502			T(x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)}(x^V)\,,
   503		\]
   504		is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U \oplus V$.
   505	\end{lemma}
   506	\begin{proof}
   507		\uses{def:cl-func}
   508		By induction on $k$. The case $k = 0$ follows directly from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, since then $L = 0$ and $T$ acts by the single $\ell$-level function $R_0$ on the register subspace $V$. For the inductive step, write $L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}})$ with complementary register subspaces $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$. For each value $x^{L_1}$, the function $T_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ sending $x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}$ to $L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) + R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V)$ is the concatenation of the $(k-1)$-level function $L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}$ with a family drawn from $\{R_u\}$, hence is $(k+\ell-1)$-level by the induction hypothesis. The claim then follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} applied with first subspace $U_1$ and first linear map $L_1$.
   509	\end{proof}

   511	% The source (references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364) leaves
   512	% the number m of summands unquantified (m >= 1 is needed for the level max_j ell_j to
   513	% have an index) and begins its induction at level 1; the level-zero base case is supplied
   514	% here, since def:cl-func admits 0-level functions and all ell_j may be 0.
   515	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   516		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   517		Let $m \ge 1$ be an integer and let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \dots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.    518		\[
   519			L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   520		\]

   546		\uses{def:cl-func}

A \emph{$\mathcal T$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_t\}_{t \in \mathcal T}$ such that, for each $t \in \mathcal T$, $L_t$ is an $\ell$-level conditionally linear function on $V$.

   553	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]\label{def:graph-distribution}
   554		Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and nonempty edge set $E$. Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of $G$} is the distribution over $U \times U$ such that for every $(u,v) \in U \times U$,
   555		\[
   556			\mu_G(u, v) =
   557			\begin{cases}
   558				1/(2m-k) & \text{if } \{u,v\} \in E\,,\\
   559				0 & \text{otherwise}\,.
   560			\end{cases}
   561		\]

    10	\section{The classical low individual degree game}
    11	% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    12	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    13	\label{sec:ld-game}
    14	
    15	The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

    17	\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\label{def:ld-game}
    18		\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}
    19		% The source fixes \N to be the set of positive integers
    20		% (references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:6) and takes m, d, ldc in \N
    21		% (references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:33-35),
    22		% so the positivity below is the source's implicit domain, stated explicitly.
    23		% It is load-bearing: at d = 0 or k = 0 the prefactor a(dmk)^a of delta_ld in
    24		% lem:ld-soundness vanishes, and at d = 0 the resulting exact conclusions fail
    25		% (e.g. at (q,m,d,k) = (2,1,0,1) with eps = 1). The case k = 0, though it would
    26		% hold trivially, is likewise outside the source's domain and is omitted.
    27		The game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m, d, k \ge 1$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. We write $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ to emphasize the dependence on the parameter tuple. The type set of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is
    28		\[
    29			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} = \{\mathsf{Point}, \mathsf{ALine}, \mathsf{DLine}\}\;,
    30		\]
    31		and the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} \times \mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}}$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.

    34	\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\label{def:ld-question-distribution}
    35		\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}
    36		Let $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
    37		\begin{equation}
    38			\label{eq:cl-ptf}
    39			L_{\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\;.
    40		\end{equation}
    41		For $s \in \F_q$, let $\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that
    42		\begin{equation}
    43			\label{eq:chi-func}
    44			s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m} + r
    45		\end{equation}
    46		for some $0 \le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}$ under the identification of $\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.     47		\begin{equation}
    48			\label{eq:cl-alnf}
    49			L_{\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\, s,\, 0\bigr)\quad\text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V\;,

    86	\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\label{def:ld-win-predicate}

   107	\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
   108		The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
   109	\end{remark}

By Definition~\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \le q-1$; at the canonical parameters (Definition~\ref{def:introparams}, where $d = 1 \le q-1$) the identification is bijective; the general statements of this chapter quantify over all admissible tuples and are read through the representative convention.    118	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.

   122	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\label{lem:ld-soundness}
   123		\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:consistency, def:bracket}
   124		There exists a function
   125		\[

   182	\section{The Magic Square game}
   183	% Paper label sec:ms kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   184	\label{sec:ms}
   185	
   186	We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test. Here it is presented as a binary constraint satisfaction game. Throughout this section and the next, $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ denote the single-qubit Pauli observables, with associated two-outcome projective measurements $\{\sigma^W_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$.
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[The Magic Square game]\label{def:ms-game}
   189		\uses{def:game, def:graph-distribution}
   190		The Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the following two-player game. There are $9$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_9$ taking values in $\F_2$, arranged in a $3 \times 3$ grid: the cell in row $r$ and column $c$ contains the variable $x_{3(r-1)+c}$. There are $6$ linear equations over these variables: for each of the three rows and each of the first two columns, the sum of the three variables in it equals $0$; for the third column, the sum of the three variables in it equals $1$.
   191	
   192		The question types are
   193		\begin{align*}
   194			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
   195			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
   196			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
   197		\end{align*}
   198		where $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ denotes the constraint of row $i$ (with variables $x_{3(i-1)+1}, x_{3(i-1)+2}, x_{3(i-1)+3}$), $\mathsf{Constraint}_4$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_5$ denote the constraints of the first two columns, and $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$ denotes the constraint of the third column (with variables $x_{i-3}, x_{i}, x_{i+3}$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$, $i \in \{4,5,6\}$).
   199	
   200		The question distribution is as follows: the verifier samples $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$, then samples $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ uniformly among the three variables appearing in the row or column of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; one player, chosen uniformly at random, receives $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and the other receives $\mathsf{Variable}_j$. Equivalently, the verifier samples a uniformly random edge of the bipartite \emph{type graph} $G^{\mathrm{ms}}$ on vertex sets $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$ and $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}$, whose edges are $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{3(i-1)+j}$ for $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{(i-3)+3(j-1)}$ for $i \in \{4,5,6\}$, $j \in \{1,2,3\}$ ($18$ edges in total, and no self-loops), and sends one endpoint to a uniformly random player and the other endpoint to the other player.
   201	
   202		The $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player answers with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; the $\mathsf{Variable}$ player answers with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$. The players win if and only if the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player's answer satisfies the equation associated with $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   203	\end{definition}
   204	
   205	The following theorem records the self-testing (rigidity) properties of the Magic Square game. It is used in the soundness analysis of the Pauli basis test to enforce anticommutation relations between certain pairs of observables.
   206	
   207	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]\label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   208		\uses{def:ms-game, def:tensor-product-value, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   209		Let $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ with probability $1-\eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B}$. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_{\mathrm A}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm A} \to \hilb_{\mathrm A'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm A''}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm B}\colon \hilb_{\mathrm B} \to \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, where $\hilb_{\mathrm A'}, \hilb_{\mathrm B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\ot 2}$ and $\hilb_{\mathrm A''}, \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$ are finite dimensional, and a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \in \hilb_{\mathrm A''} \ot \hilb_{\mathrm B''}$, such that:
   210		\begin{enumerate}
   211			\item $\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm A} \ot \phi_{\mathrm B} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \bigr\| \le O(\sqrt\eps)$;
   212			\item letting $\tilde A^x_a = \phi_{\mathrm A} A^x_a \phi_{\mathrm A}^\dagger$ and $\tilde B^y_b = \phi_{\mathrm B} B^y_b \phi_{\mathrm B}^\dagger$,
   213			\begin{align*}
   214				\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^X_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
   215				\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} (\sigma^Z_b)_{\mathrm A'} \ot I_{\mathrm{A''B'B''}}\;,\\
   216				I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} I_{\mathrm{A'A''B''}} \ot (\sigma^X_b)_{\mathrm B'}\;,\\
   217				I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} I_{\mathrm{A'A''B''}} \ot (\sigma^Z_b)_{\mathrm B'}\;,
   218			\end{align*}
   219			where each $\approx_{\sqrt\eps}$ holds with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2}_{\mathrm{A'B'}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A''B''}}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$, and the approximation bounds carry implicit universal constants.
   220		\end{enumerate}
   221		As a consequence, letting $\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} = \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_0 - \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_1$ and $\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} = \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_0 - \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_1$ denote the associated observables, it holds that
   222		\begin{align*}
   223			\tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} -\, \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \tilde A^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \ot I_{\mathrm{B'B''}}\;,\\
   224			I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1} \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} &\approx_{\sqrt\eps} -\, I_{\mathrm{A'A''}} \ot \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_5} \tilde B^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}\;,
   225		\end{align*}
   226		where, for operators $M$, $N$ that are not POVM elements, the notation $M \approx_\delta N$ means $\bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi} \le O(\delta)$ with respect to the same state.
   227	\end{theorem}
   228	\begin{proof}
   229		This result is imported from Theorem~6.9 of~\cite{Coladangelo2017Robust}. There are two minor differences between their statement and the one given here. First, they state a robustness of $O(\eps)$, but measure the closeness of the actual and ideal states in trace norm; expressed as the Euclidean distance between $\phi_{\mathrm A} \ot \phi_{\mathrm B}\ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}^{\ot 2} \ot \ket{\mathrm{aux}}$, this becomes $O(\sqrt\eps)$. Second, their ideal observables for the $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$ questions are $I \ot \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^Z\sigma^X \ot \sigma^Z\sigma^X$; under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \ot I$ and $\sigma^Z \ot I$, respectively.
   230	\end{proof}
   231	
   232	The converse construction shows that any pair of anticommuting binary observables yields a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game.
   233	
   234	\begin{theorem}\label{thm:ms-from-ac}
   235		\uses{def:ms-game, def:consistent-measurement, def:spcc, def:EPR, def:tensor-product-value}
   236		Let $A = \{A_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ and $B = \{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ be two-outcome projective measurements acting on $(\C^q)^{\ot n}$ that are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement}), and let $\mathcal O_A = A_0 - A_1$ and $\mathcal O_B = B_0 - B_1$ be the corresponding $\pm 1$-valued observables. Suppose that $\mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B = - \mathcal O_B \mathcal O_A$. Then there exists a symmetric strategy $\mathcal S = (\psi, M)$ for the Magic Square game with the following properties:
   237		\begin{enumerate}
   238			\item $\mathcal S$ is an SPCC (symmetric, projective, consistent, commuting) strategy of value $1$;
   239			\item the state is $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$;
   240			\item for $b \in \{0,1\}$, $M^{\mathsf{Variable}_1}_b = A_b \ot I$ and $M^{\mathsf{Variable}_5}_b = B_b \ot I$.
   241		\end{enumerate}
   242	\end{theorem}
   243	\begin{proof}
   244		\uses{def:consistent-measurement}
   245		The strategy is based on the canonical two-qubit operator solution of the Magic Square, with the state $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ and the cells of the grid assigned the $\pm 1$-valued observables
   246		\[
   247			\begin{array}{ccc}
   248				\mathcal O_A \ot I & I \ot \sigma^X & \mathcal O_A \ot \sigma^X \\[2pt]
   249				I \ot \sigma^Z & \mathcal O_B \ot I & \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^Z \\[2pt]
   250				\mathcal O_A \ot \sigma^Z & \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^X & \mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^Z \sigma^X
   251			\end{array}
   252		\]
   253		on $(\C^q)^{\ot n} \ot \C^2$: on question $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ a player measures the two-outcome projective measurement of the observable in cell $j$, and on question $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ a player simultaneously performs the three measurements of the corresponding row or column; item~3 holds by construction. Anticommutation of $\mathcal O_A$ and $\mathcal O_B$ gives
   254		\begin{equation}\label{eq:am-i-hermitian}
   255			\mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^Z \sigma^X
   256			= - \mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   257			= \mathcal O_B \mathcal O_A \ot \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   258			= (\mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B \ot \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^\dagger\;,
   259		\end{equation}
   260		so the bottom-right cell is Hermitian, and it squares to the identity; hence every cell is a genuine $\pm 1$-valued observable. The three observables in each row and each column commute pairwise --- for the third row and third column this again uses Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian} --- so the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ measurements are well defined, and the strategy is symmetric, projective, and commuting. A two-outcome projective measurement is consistent on a state if and only if its observable $\mathcal O$ satisfies $\mathcal O \ot I \ket{\psi} = I \ot \mathcal O \ket{\psi}$; since $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot n}$ by hypothesis and $\sigma^X$, $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$, each cell observable is a product of consistent, commuting factors and is therefore consistent on $\ket{\psi}$, and consistency of the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ measurements follows from the cellwise consistencies together with commutativity. Finally, the observables in each row and each of the first two columns multiply to $I$, while those of the third column multiply to $-I$; for the measurement $\{S_0, S_1\}$ obtained by measuring a $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ triple and outputting the sum of the three bits, the observable $S_0 - S_1$ equals the product of the three cell observables, hence $\pm I$, which forces the three answer bits to sum to $0$ (respectively, $1$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$) with certainty. Together with consistency this shows that every check of the Magic Square game is passed with probability $1$, so the strategy has value $1$.
   261	\end{proof}

   263	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   264	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   265	\label{sec:qld-game}
   266	
   267	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
   268

   371	\begin{lemma}[Completeness of the Pauli basis test]\label{lem:pauli-completeness}

   373		For every admissible tuple $\mathsf{qldparams} = (q,m,d)$ (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), the Pauli basis test $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$ has a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
   374	\end{lemma}

   376		\uses{thm:ms-from-ac, def:pauli-win-predicate, def:bracket, def:consistent-measurement, def:EPR, def:indicator-vector, lem:pauli-observable-expansion, lem:twisted-commutation}
   377		The strategy uses the state $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ with $M = 2^m$. On a question $((\mathsf{Point},W), y)$ a player measures the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ and reports $g_h(y)$; on $((\mathsf{ALine},W), \ell)$ or $((\mathsf{DLine},W), \ell)$ they report the restriction of $g_h$ to the line $\ell$, expressed as a univariate polynomial through the canonical parameterization of $\ell$; and on $(\mathsf{Pauli},W)$ they report $h$ itself --- in the bracket notation of Definition~\ref{def:bracket}, these measurements are $\tau^W_{[g_\cdot(y) = a]} \ot I$, $\tau^W_{[(g_\cdot)|_\ell = f]} \ot I$, and $\tau^W_a \ot I$. For a content $\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z)$, consider the two binary measurements $A_b = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_\cdot(u_X)\, r_X) = b]} \ot I$ and $B_b = \tau^Z_{[\tr(g_\cdot(u_Z)\, r_Z) = b]} \ot I$. Since $g_h(u) = h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}), the relation between the Pauli projections and observables gives $\mathcal O_A = A_0 - A_1 = \tau^X(\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)\, r_X) \ot I$ and $\mathcal O_B = \tau^Z(\mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)\, r_Z) \ot I$, and the twisted commutation relation yields
   378		\[
   379			\mathcal O_A \mathcal O_B = (-1)^\gamma\, \mathcal O_B \mathcal O_A
   380		\]
   381		with $\gamma$ as in Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}: the two measurements commute when $\gamma = 0$ and anticommute when $\gamma = 1$. If $\gamma = 0$, define $E^{\mathsf{Pair},\omega}_{\beta_X,\beta_Z} = A_{\beta_X} B_{\beta_Z}$ and $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},X),\omega}_a = A_a$, $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},Z),\omega}_a = B_a$, and let the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ and $\mathsf{Variable}$ measurements be trivial (identity on the all-zeros outcome). If $\gamma = 1$, let the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ and $\mathsf{Variable}$ measurements be those produced by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac} from the anticommuting consistent pair $(A, B)$, acting on the auxiliary $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ factor, and let the $\mathsf{Pair}$ measurements be trivial. The strategy is symmetric and projective by construction; every measurement is either a post-processed Pauli basis measurement, a measurement supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, or (in the $\gamma = 0$ case) a product of two commuting consistent measurements, so the strategy is consistent, and commutativity along every edge of $G^{\mathrm{pauli}}$ is checked case by case --- for instance, $(\mathsf{Point},X)$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ commute because both are $X$-basis measurements. Consistency and projectivity give the consistency checks with certainty, and the low-degree checks pass because the answers agree with the strategy determined by the polynomial $g_h$ in the classical game. For the remaining checks: when $\gamma = 0$ the commutation check passes by construction, and when $\gamma = 1$ the Magic Square check passes by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}; the consistency checks 5 and 7 pass with certainty because $\tau^W_{[\tr(g_\cdot(y)\, r_W) = \cdot]} \ot I$ coincides with $E^{(\mathsf{Pair},W),\omega}$, respectively with the embedded $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$ measurements of Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac} (item~3 there). Hence the strategy has value $1$.

   420	\subsection{Finite fields}
   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   556	
   557	\begin{lemma}
   558	  \label{lem:downsize_subspace}
   559	  Let $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ denote the map corresponding to a
   560	  basis $\{e_i\}$ for $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   561	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_{q^k}^n$ with linearly independent basis
   562	  $\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\} \subseteq \F_{q^k}^n$.
   563	  Then the following hold:
   564	  \begin{enumerate}
   565	 	\item $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace of $\,\F_{q}^{nk}$.
   566		\item $\{ \downsize_q(e_i b_j) \}_{i,j}$ is a linearly independent basis of
   567	    $\downsize_q(V)$ over $\F_q$.
   568		\item Let $V, W$ be complementary subspaces of $\F_{q^k}^n$.
   569	    Then $V' = \downsize_q(V)$ and $W' = \downsize_q(W)$ are complementary
   570	    subspaces of $\F_q^{kn}$, and furthermore for all vectors $z \in
   571	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsize_q(z^V) = \downsize_q(z)^{V'}$ and
   572	    $\downsize_q(z^W) = \downsize_q(z)^{W'}$.
   573	  \end{enumerate}
   574	\end{lemma}
   575	
   576	\begin{proof}
   577	  For the first item, we first verify that $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace.
   578	  Since $V$ is a subspace, it contains $0 \in \F_{q^k}^n$, and therefore $\downsize_q(0)
   579	  = 0$ is also in $\downsize_q(V)$.
   580	  Let $u', v' \in \downsize_q(V)$.
   581	  Using that $\downsize_q$ is a bijection there exist $u,v \in \F_{q^k}^n$ such that
   582	  $u' = \downsize_q(u)$ and $v' = \downsize_q(v)$. Therefore
   583	  \[
   584	    u' + v' = \downsize_q(u) + \downsize_q(v) =
   585	    \downsize_q(u + v) \in \downsize_q(V)\;,
   586	  \]
   587	  where the inclusion follows because $V$ is a subspace and thus contains $u +
   588	  v$.
   589	  Finally, for all $x' \in \F_{q}$, for all $v \in V$, we have that $x'
   590	  \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(x' v)\in \downsize_q(V)$ where we used that $V$
   591	  is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q^k}$ and thus by $\F_q$ (since
   592	  $\F_q$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$).
   593	  Thus $\downsize_q(V)$ is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q}$.
   594	
   595	  For the second item, note that an element $v \in V$ can be expressed uniquely
   596	  as $v = \sum_{i = 1}^t v_i b_i$ for $v_i \in \F_{q^k}$.
   597	  The element $v_i$ can further be written as $\sum_j v_{i, j} e_j$ where $v_{i,
   598	    j} \in \F_q$.
   599	  Thus $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ e_j b_i \}$, and therefore
   600	  $\downsize_q(v)$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ \downsize_q (e_j
   601	  b_i) \}$.
   602	  To establish that the vectors $\{ \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \}$ are linearly
   603	  independent, suppose towards contradiction that they are not.
   604	  Then there would exist $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that at least one
   605	  $\alpha_{i, j}$ is nonzero and
   606	  \begin{align*}
   607	    0 & = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \\
   608	      & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl (\sum_j \alpha_{i, j}
   609	        e_j \bigr) b_i \Bigr) \\
   610	      & = \downsize_q \left ( \sum_i \beta_i b_i \right ),
   611	  \end{align*}
   612	  where we define $\beta_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   613	  Since at least one $\alpha_{i, j} \neq 0$ and the $\{e_j\}$ are linearly
   614	  independent over $\F_q$, there exists $i$ such that $\beta_i \neq 0$, which
   615	  means that there is a non-trivial linear combination of the basis elements
   616	  $b_i$ that equals $0$ under $\downsize_q(\cdot)$.
   617	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is injective, we get a contradiction with linear
   618	  independence of the $\{b_i\}$.
   619	
   620	  For the third item, we observe that $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$ must
   621	  be complementary because $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a linear map as well as a
   622	  bijection.
   623	  Let $\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}$ and $\{v_{m+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ denote bases for $V$ and
   624	  $W$, respectively.
   625	  Thus the set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$ forms a basis for $\F_{q^k}^n$, and from the
   626	  previous item, the set $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{i,\, j}$ is a basis for
   627	  $\F_q^{kn}$.
   628	  Furthermore, the sets $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\,i = 1,\ldots m}$ and
   629	  $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\, i = m+1,\ldots n}$ are bases for
   630	  $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$, respectively.
   631	
   632	  There is a unique choice of coefficients $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that
   633	  $\downsize_q(z) = \sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j v_i)$.
   634	  But then
   635	  \begin{align*}
   636	    \downsize_q(z) & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl ( \sum_j
   637	                     \alpha_{i, j} e_j \bigr) v_i \Bigr) \\
   638	                   & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \alpha_i v_i \Bigr)\;,
   639	  \end{align*}
   640	  where we define $\alpha_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly
   643	  $z^W = \sum_{i=m+1}^n \alpha_i v_i$).
   644	  This implies that
   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}
   649	  and similarly $\downsize_q(z)^{W'} = \downsize_q(z^W)$.
   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =

   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   926	\subsection{Linear spaces and registers}
   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]

  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,

    35	\begin{definition}
    36	  \label{def:cl-func}
    37		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$.
    38	  For all integers $\ell\geq 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level
    39	    conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined
    40	  inductively as follows.
    41	  \begin{enumerate}
    42	  \item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the
    43	    $0$ function on $V$.
    44	
    45	  \item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level
    46	    conditionally linear functions has been defined.
    47	    The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists
    48	    of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form.
    49	    There exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a
    50	    linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an
    51	    $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\, v}$ on $V_{>1}$,
    52	    such that for all $x\in V$,
    53	    \begin{equation*}
    54	      L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}} (x^{V_{>1}})\;.
    55	    \end{equation*}
