   263	/-- A finite edge set for the typed Pauli question graph.  The self-loops and
   264	the displayed type-incidence families are the graph used by the sampler in
   265	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint lines 285-329, paper origin
   266	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   267	-/
   268	def pauliEdges : Finset (Sym2 PauliType) :=
   269	  let loops := Finset.univ.image (fun t : PauliType => Sym2.mk t t)
   270	  let lineEdges :=
   271	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   272	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.aline W)) ∪
   273	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   274	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.dline W)) ∪
   275	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   276	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pauli W))
   277	  let basisEdges :=
   278	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   279	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pairW W)) ∪
   280	      ({Sym2.mk (.point .X) (.ms (.var ⟨0, by decide⟩)),
   281	        Sym2.mk (.point .Z) (.ms (.var ⟨4, by decide⟩))} : Finset (Sym2 PauliType))
   282	  let pairEdges :=
   283	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   284	      Sym2.mk (.pairW W) .pair)
   285	  let msEdges' :=
   286	    (Finset.univ : Finset (MsType × MsType)).filter (fun xy =>
   287	      Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges) |>.image (fun xy =>
   288	        Sym2.mk (.ms xy.1) (.ms xy.2))
   289	  loops ∪ lineEdges ∪ basisEdges ∪ pairEdges ∪ msEdges'
   290	
   291	/-- A Pauli question is a type together with a full ambient coefficient vector
   292	(`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper
   293	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
   294	-/
   295	abbrev PauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliType × PauliSpace P
   296	
   297	/-- The ordered-edge subtype used by the Pauli question sampler.  This is
   298	the finite carrier underlying `graphDistribution pauliEdges`; it is Lean-only
   299	infrastructure for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   300	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   301	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   302	-/
   303	abbrev PauliEdge :=
   304	  {e : PauliType × PauliType // Sym2.mk e.1 e.2 ∈ pauliEdges}
   305	
   306	/-- The Pauli graph has a loop, so its ordered-edge subtype is nonempty.  This
   307	is a finite-carrier fact used only to instantiate the uniform source sampler
   308	for `def:pauli-question-distribution`; the graph itself is the source-facing
   309	object `pauliEdges` above (same blueprint and paper references).
   310	-/
   311	theorem pauliEdge_nonempty : Nonempty PauliEdge := by
   312	  refine ⟨⟨(.point .X, .point .X), ?_⟩⟩
   313	  simp [pauliEdges]
   314	
   315	/-- The Pauli question distribution from `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   316	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   317	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1070-1120`.
   318	-/
   319	noncomputable def pauliQuestionDistribution (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   320	    Distribution (PauliQuestion P × PauliQuestion P) :=
   321	  by
   322	    classical
   323	    letI : Nonempty PauliEdge := pauliEdge_nonempty
   324	    exact
   325	      Distribution.map
   326	        (uniformDistribution (PauliEdge × PauliSpace P))
   327	        (fun s =>
   328	          ((s.1.1.1, pauliCL P s.1.1.1 s.2),
   329	            (s.1.1.2, pauliCL P s.1.1.2 s.2)))
   330	
   331	/-- The finite answer alphabet for the Pauli basis test.  Its constructors are
   332	the seven answer forms in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint lines 331-367,
   333	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   334	-/
   335	inductive PauliAnswer (P : AdmissibleParams) where
   336	  | value (a : PauliScalar P)
   337	  | alinePoly (a : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   338	  | dlinePoly (a : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   339	  | pairBits (a : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)
   340	  | bit (a : ZMod 2)
   341	  | msTriple (a : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
   342	  | pauliOutcome (a : PauliRegister P)
   343	  deriving DecidableEq
   344	
   345	/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the
   346	answer alphabet in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   347	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   348	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   349	-/
   350	abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   351	  PauliScalar P ⊕
   352	    ((Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   353	      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   354	        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
   355	          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))
   356	
   357	/-- The constructor-preserving finite-code equivalence for `PauliAnswer`.
   358	Lean-only infrastructure for `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   359	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   360	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.

361	-/
   362	noncomputable def pauliAnswerEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   363	    PauliAnswer P ≃ PauliAnswerCode P where
   364	  toFun
   365	    | .value a => .inl a
   366	    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
   367	    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
   368	    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
   369	    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))
   370	    | .msTriple a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))))
   371	    | .pauliOutcome a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a)))))
   372	  invFun
   373	    | .inl a => .value a
   374	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePoly a
   375	    | .inr (.inr (.inl a)) => .dlinePoly a
   376	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))) => .pairBits a
   377	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))) => .bit a
   378	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))) => .msTriple a
   379	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a))))) => .pauliOutcome a
   380	  left_inv := by
   381	    intro x
   382	    cases x <;> rfl
   383	  right_inv := by
   384	    intro x
   385	    cases x with
   386	    | inl a => rfl
   387	    | inr x =>
   388	        cases x with
   389	        | inl a => rfl
   390	        | inr x =>
   391	            cases x with
   392	            | inl a => rfl
   393	            | inr x =>
   394	                cases x with
   395	                | inl a => rfl
   396	                | inr x =>
   397	                    cases x with
   398	                    | inl a => rfl
   399	                    | inr x =>
   400	                        cases x with
   401	                        | inl a => rfl
   402	                        | inr a => rfl
   403	
   404	noncomputable instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Fintype (PauliAnswer P) :=
   405	  Fintype.ofEquiv (PauliAnswerCode P) (pauliAnswerEquiv P).symm
   406	
   407	instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Inhabited (PauliAnswer P) :=
   408	  ⟨.bit 0⟩
   409	
   410	/-- The phase bit `γ(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)` from `eq:gamma-value`.  It uses the
   411	fixed trace selected by `P.model`, as required by the paper's fixed
   412	self-dual-normal representation.  Blueprint
   413	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   414	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   415	-/
   416	noncomputable def gammaValue (P : AdmissibleParams)
   417	    (uX uZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   418	    (rX rZ : PauliScalar P) : ZMod 2 :=
   419	  fixedBinTrace P.model
   420	    (dotProduct (rX • indicatorVec uX) (rZ • indicatorVec uZ))
   421	
   422	/-- The commutation bit attached to a full Pauli ambient question, from
   423	`eq:gamma-value` in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   424	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   425	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   426	-/
   427	noncomputable def pauliPairGamma (P : AdmissibleParams) (z : PauliSpace P) : ZMod 2 :=
   428	  gammaValue P (pauliXBlock z) (pauliZBlock z)
   429	    (pauliRXBlock z) (pauliRZBlock z)
   430	
   431	/-- The answer constructor prescribed by each Pauli question type; this is the
   432	well-formedness part of `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   433	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   434	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   435	-/
   436	def validPauliAnswer {P : AdmissibleParams} (t : PauliType) (a : PauliAnswer P) : Bool :=
   437	  match t, a with
   438	  | .point _, .value _ => true
   439	  | .aline _, .alinePoly _ => true
   440	  | .dline _, .dlinePoly _ => true
   441	  | .pauli _, .pauliOutcome _ => true
   442	  | .pairW _, .bit _ => true
   443	  | .pair, .pairBits _ => true
   444	  | .ms (.constraint _), .msTriple _ => true
   445	  | .ms (.var _), .bit _ => true
   446	  | _, _ => false
   447	
   448	/-- The axis-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   449	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   450	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   451	-/
   452	def pauliAlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   453	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   454	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   455	  -- The universal form preserves the source's zero-direction convention.
   456	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   457	    pauliPointBlock W point =
   458	        pauliPointBlock W line + t • coordinateDirection
   459	          (chiIndex P.toLdParams (pauliScalarBlock line)) →
   460	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   461	
   462	/-- The diagonal-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   463	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   464	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   465	-/
   466	def pauliDlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   467	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   468	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   469	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   470	    pauliPointBlock W point = pauliPointBlock W line +
   471	        t • pauliDirectionBlock line →
   472	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   473	
   474	/-- The raw Pauli-versus-point consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   475	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   476	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   477	-/
   478	def pauliPointPauliCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   479	    (point : PauliSpace P) (h : PauliRegister P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   480	  lowDegreeEnc h (pauliPointBlock W point) = a
   481	
   482	/-- The Pair/W consistency relation, including the one-sided gamma gate, from
   483	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   484	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   485	-/
   486	def pauliPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   487	    (z : PauliSpace P) (β : ZMod 2) (bits : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   488	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   489	    (match W with
   490	    | .X => bits.1 = β
   491	    | .Z => bits.2 = β)
   492	
   493	/-- The point/Pair/W trace consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   494	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   495	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   496	-/
   497	def pauliPointPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   498	    (z : PauliSpace P) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   499	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   500	    fixedBinTrace P.model
   501	      (a * (match W with
   502	      | .X => pauliRXBlock z
   503	      | .Z => pauliRZBlock z)) = β
   504	
   505	/-- The Point/Variable consistency clause of `def:pauli-win-predicate`.
   506	The check is gated by `gamma = 0` and only uses Variable 1 in the X basis or
   507	Variable 5 in the Z basis.  Blueprint
   508	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   509	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   510	-/
   511	def pauliPointVariableCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   512	    (z : PauliSpace P) (j : Fin 9) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   513	  pauliPairGamma P z = 0 ∨
   514	    (j = ⟨0, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .X ∧
   515	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRXBlock z) = β) ∨
   516	    (j = ⟨4, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .Z ∧
   517	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRZBlock z) = β)
   518	
   519	/-- The Pauli win predicate, with constructor-shape rejection.  This is
   520	`def:pauli-win-predicate` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`,
   521	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   522	-/
   523	noncomputable def pauliWinPredicate (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   524	    PauliQuestion P → PauliQuestion P → PauliAnswer P → PauliAnswer P → Bool :=
   525	  open Classical in
   526	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   527	    if validPauliAnswer tA a && validPauliAnswer tB b then
   528	      if tA = tB then
   529	        decide (a = b)
   530	      else
   531	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   532	      | .aline W, .point W', .alinePoly f, .value u =>
   533	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   534	      | .point W, .aline W', .value u, .alinePoly f =>
   535	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   536	      | .dline W, .point W', .dlinePoly f, .value u =>
   537	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   538	      | .point W, .dline W', .value u, .dlinePoly f =>
   539	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   540	      | .point W, .pauli W', .value u, .pauliOutcome h =>
   541	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xA h u) else true
   542	      | .pauli W, .point W', .pauliOutcome h, .value u =>
   543	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xB h u) else true
   544	      | .pairW W, .pair, .bit β, .pairBits bits =>
   545	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xA β bits)
   546	      | .pair, .pairW W, .pairBits bits, .bit β =>
   547	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xB β bits)
   548	      | .point W, .pairW W', .value u, .bit β =>
   549	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xB u β) else true
   550	      | .pairW W, .point W', .bit β, .value u =>
   551	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xA u β) else true
   552	      | .ms (.constraint i), .ms (.var j), .msTriple β, .bit γ =>
   553	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   554	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
   555	              msWinPredicate (.constraint i) (.var j) (.triple β) (.bit γ))
   556	          else true
   557	      | .ms (.var j), .ms (.constraint i), .bit γ, .msTriple β =>
   558	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   559	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xB = 0 ∨
   560	              msWinPredicate (.var j) (.constraint i) (.bit γ) (.triple β))
   561	          else true
   562	      | .point W, .ms (.var j), .value u, .bit β =>
   563	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xB j u β)
   564	      | .ms (.var j), .point W, .bit β, .value u =>
   565	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xA j u β)
   566	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   567	    else false
   568	
   569	/-- The Pauli basis test game.  This is `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
   570	`def:pauli-win-predicate` packaged as the symmetric game of
   571	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-367`, paper origin
   572	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1225`.
   573	-/
   574	noncomputable def pauliBasisTest (P : AdmissibleParams) : Game where
   575	  QuestionA := PauliQuestion P
   576	  QuestionB := PauliQuestion P
   577	  AnswerA := PauliAnswer P
   578	  AnswerB := PauliAnswer P
   579	  μ := pauliQuestionDistribution P
   580	  μ_prob := by sorry
   581	  decide := pauliWinPredicate P
   582	
   583	end
   584	
   585	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

    37	structure LdParams where

    41	  k : ℕ
    42	  hm : 1 ≤ m
    43	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    44	  hk : 1 ≤ k

    48	/-- The fixed model accessor for an `LdParams` record.  It is a compatibility
    49	view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently quantified

    53	noncomputable def LdParams.model (P : LdParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=

    56	/-- The scalar carrier selected by an `LdParams` record; this is the fixed
    57	field carrier in `def:ld-game`, selected globally by `LdParams.model`.

    59	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

    61	abbrev ScalarQ (P : LdParams) := (P.model).K
    62	
    63	/-- The three low-degree question types of `def:ld-game`, blueprint
    64	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    65	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    66	-/
    67	inductive LdType where
    68	  | point
    69	  | aline
    70	  | dline
    71	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    72	
    73	/-- The register index used by the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    74	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
    76	-/
    77	abbrev LdIndex (P : LdParams) := (Fin P.m ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m
    78	
    79	/-- The full ambient low-degree coefficient space (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    80	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    81	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
    82	-/
    83	abbrev LdSpace (P : LdParams) := LdIndex P → ScalarQ P

    85	/-- The point coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    87	-/
    88	def LdSpace.point {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
    89	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl i))
    90	
    91	/-- The shared scalar coordinate of an ambient low-degree vector in
    92	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

    94	def LdSpace.seed {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : ScalarQ P :=

   291	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →

   295	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin

   299	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   300	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=

   305	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   306	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   307	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   308	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   310	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   311	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   312	  open Classical in
   313	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   314	      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
   315	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   316	        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
   317	        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   318	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   319	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   320	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   321	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   322	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   323	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   324	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   325	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   326	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   327	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   328	      else false

340		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   341		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   342		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   343		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   344		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   345		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   346		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   347		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   348		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   349	\end{definition}
   350	
   351	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   352		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   353		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   354		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   355		most $d$. Then
   356		\[
   357			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   358		\]
   359	\end{lemma}
   360	\begin{proof}
   361		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   362		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   363		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   364		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   365	\end{proof}
   366	
   367	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   368		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   369		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   370		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   371		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   372		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of
   373		$\F_q^m$; the analysis of the Pauli basis test uses the bound in this
   374		individual-degree form.
   375	\end{remark}
   376	
   377	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   378	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   379	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   380	
   381	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   382		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   383		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   384		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   385		\[
   386			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   387			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   388		\]
   389		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   390		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   391		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   392		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   393		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   394		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   395		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   396		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   397			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   398		\end{equation}
   399		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   400		degree at most $m$.
   401	\end{definition}
   402	
   403	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   404		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   405		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   406		\[
   407			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   408			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   409		\]
   410		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   411		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   412		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   413		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   414			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   415		\end{equation}
   416		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   417	\end{definition}
   418	
   419	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   420	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   421	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   422	
   423	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   424		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   425		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   426		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   427		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   428		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   429		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   430		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   431	\end{definition}

   433	\section{Lines}
   434	
   435	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   436	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   437	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   438	
   439	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   440		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   442		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   443			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   444		\end{equation}
   445		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   446		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   447		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   449		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   450		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   453	\end{definition}
   454	
   455	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   456		\uses{def:line}
   457		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   458		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   459	\end{proposition}
   460	\begin{proof}
   461		\uses{def:line}
   462		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   463		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   464		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   465		inclusion.
   466	\end{proof}
   467	
   468	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   469	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   470	representation is obtained as follows.
   471	
   472	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   473		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   474		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   475		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   476		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   477		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   478		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   479		\[
   480			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   481		\]
   482		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   483		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   484		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   485		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   486		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   487		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   488		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   489		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   490		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   491		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   492	\end{definition}

   498	\begin{definition}[State space of a linear register]\label{def:lin-reg}
   499		\uses{def:complementary}
   500		For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension
   501		$|V|$, endowed with the canonical orthonormal basis
   502		$\{\ket{x}\}_{x \in V}$. A \emph{quantum state on $V$} is a unit vector
   503		$\ket{\psi}_V \in \C^V$. If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_i$ is a direct sum of
   504		subspaces over $\F$, then $\C^V$ is identified with
   505		$\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{V_i}$ by identifying
   506		$\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k}$ with
   507		$\ket{x_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{x_k}$. In particular, a basis $\{e_i\}$ of
   508		$V$ yields the decomposition $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k (\F e_i)$ and hence
   509		$\C^V = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{|\F|}$; the factors $\C^{|\F|}$ are called
   510		the \emph{qudits} of $\C^V$.
   511	\end{definition}

   513	\begin{definition}[EPR state]\label{def:EPR}
   514		\uses{def:lin-reg}

   516		$\C^V \ot \C^V$ is
   517		\[
   518			\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_V
   519			= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|V|}} \sum_{x \in V} \ket{x} \ot \ket{x}\;.
   520		\]

   522		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
   523	\end{definition}

     4	This chapter records the algebraic preliminaries needed for the quantum Pauli
     5	basis test, following the preliminaries of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}: subspace
     6	machinery over finite fields (which underlies the conditionally linear question
     7	distributions of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}), field extensions, traces, and

     9	Pauli observables together with the EPR states they act on. Measurements,

    14	\section{Linear spaces and subspaces}
    15	% Paper label sec:linear-spaces kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    26		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    27		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    28		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    29	\end{definition}
    30	
    31	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    32		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    33		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    34		\[
    35			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    36		\]
    37		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    38		\[
    39			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    40		\]
    41		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    42	\end{definition}
    43	
    44	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    45	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    46	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    47	nevertheless holds over every field.
    48	
    49	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    50		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    51		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    52		\[
    53			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    54		\]
    55	\end{lemma}
    56	\begin{proof}
    57		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    58		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    59		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    60		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    61		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    62		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    63		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    64	\end{proof}
    65	
    66	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    67		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    68		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    69		\[
    70			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    71		\]
    72		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    73		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    74		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    75		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    76		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    77	\end{definition}
    78	
    79	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    82	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}
   132	
   133	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   134		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   135		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   136		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   137		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   138		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   139		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   140		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   141		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   142		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   143		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   144		$\ker(L) = S$.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   148		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   149		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   150		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   151		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   152		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   153		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   154	\end{definition}
   155	
   156	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   157		\uses{def:Lperp}
   158		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map, $F$ a basis for
   159		$\ker(L)^\perp$, and $L^\perp$ as in Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}. Then
   160		$\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   161	\end{lemma}
   162	\begin{proof}
   163		\uses{def:Lperp, def:cl-canonical, lem:canonical-complement}
   164		Set $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$;
   165		by Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement} every $v \in V$ decomposes uniquely
   166		as $v = v^S + v^T$, and by definition $L^\perp v = v^T$. If
   167		$L^\perp v = 0$ then $v = v^S \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$. Conversely, if
   168		$v \in S$ then $v^T = 0$, so $L^\perp v = 0$.
   169	\end{proof}

   171	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   172	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   173	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   174	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   175	\label{sec:subfields}
   176	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   177	
   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.

180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}
   209	
   210	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   211		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   212	\end{definition}
   213	
   214	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   215	test.
   216	
   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}
   233	
   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   241		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   242		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   243		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   244		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   245		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   246	\end{definition}
   247	
   248	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   249		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   250			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   251		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   252		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   253		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   254		\begin{enumerate}
   255			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   257			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   258			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   260			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   261			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   262		\end{enumerate}
   263		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	\begin{proof}
   266		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   267		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   268		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   269		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   270		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   271		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   272		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   273		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   274		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   275	\end{proof}
   276	
   277	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   278		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   279		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   280		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   281		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   282		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   283	\end{lemma}
   284	\begin{proof}
   285		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   290		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   292		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   293		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   296	\end{proof}
   297	
   298	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   299		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   300			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   302		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   303		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   305		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

420	\subsection{Finite fields}
   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   556	
   557	\begin{lemma}
   558	  \label{lem:downsize_subspace}
   559	  Let $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ denote the map corresponding to a
   560	  basis $\{e_i\}$ for $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   561	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_{q^k}^n$ with linearly independent basis
   562	  $\{b_1,\ldots,b_t\} \subseteq \F_{q^k}^n$.
   563	  Then the following hold:
   564	  \begin{enumerate}
   565	 	\item $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace of $\,\F_{q}^{nk}$.
   566		\item $\{ \downsize_q(e_i b_j) \}_{i,j}$ is a linearly independent basis of
   567	    $\downsize_q(V)$ over $\F_q$.
   568		\item Let $V, W$ be complementary subspaces of $\F_{q^k}^n$.
   569	    Then $V' = \downsize_q(V)$ and $W' = \downsize_q(W)$ are complementary
   570	    subspaces of $\F_q^{kn}$, and furthermore for all vectors $z \in
   571	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsize_q(z^V) = \downsize_q(z)^{V'}$ and
   572	    $\downsize_q(z^W) = \downsize_q(z)^{W'}$.
   573	  \end{enumerate}
   574	\end{lemma}
   575	
   576	\begin{proof}
   577	  For the first item, we first verify that $\downsize_q(V)$ is a subspace.
   578	  Since $V$ is a subspace, it contains $0 \in \F_{q^k}^n$, and therefore $\downsize_q(0)
   579	  = 0$ is also in $\downsize_q(V)$.
   580	  Let $u', v' \in \downsize_q(V)$.
   581	  Using that $\downsize_q$ is a bijection there exist $u,v \in \F_{q^k}^n$ such that
   582	  $u' = \downsize_q(u)$ and $v' = \downsize_q(v)$. Therefore
   583	  \[
   584	    u' + v' = \downsize_q(u) + \downsize_q(v) =
   585	    \downsize_q(u + v) \in \downsize_q(V)\;,
   586	  \]
   587	  where the inclusion follows because $V$ is a subspace and thus contains $u +
   588	  v$.
   589	  Finally, for all $x' \in \F_{q}$, for all $v \in V$, we have that $x'
   590	  \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(x' v)\in \downsize_q(V)$ where we used that $V$
   591	  is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q^k}$ and thus by $\F_q$ (since
   592	  $\F_q$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$).
   593	  Thus $\downsize_q(V)$ is closed under scalar multiplication by $\F_{q}$.
   594	
   595	  For the second item, note that an element $v \in V$ can be expressed uniquely
   596	  as $v = \sum_{i = 1}^t v_i b_i$ for $v_i \in \F_{q^k}$.
   597	  The element $v_i$ can further be written as $\sum_j v_{i, j} e_j$ where $v_{i,
   598	    j} \in \F_q$.
   599	  Thus $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ e_j b_i \}$, and therefore
   600	  $\downsize_q(v)$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\{ \downsize_q (e_j
   601	  b_i) \}$.
   602	  To establish that the vectors $\{ \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \}$ are linearly
   603	  independent, suppose towards contradiction that they are not.
   604	  Then there would exist $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that at least one
   605	  $\alpha_{i, j}$ is nonzero and
   606	  \begin{align*}
   607	    0 & = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j b_i) \\
   608	      & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl (\sum_j \alpha_{i, j}
   609	        e_j \bigr) b_i \Bigr) \\
   610	      & = \downsize_q \left ( \sum_i \beta_i b_i \right ),
   611	  \end{align*}
   612	  where we define $\beta_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   613	  Since at least one $\alpha_{i, j} \neq 0$ and the $\{e_j\}$ are linearly
   614	  independent over $\F_q$, there exists $i$ such that $\beta_i \neq 0$, which
   615	  means that there is a non-trivial linear combination of the basis elements
   616	  $b_i$ that equals $0$ under $\downsize_q(\cdot)$.
   617	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is injective, we get a contradiction with linear
   618	  independence of the $\{b_i\}$.
   619	
   620	  For the third item, we observe that $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$ must
   621	  be complementary because $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a linear map as well as a
   622	  bijection.
   623	  Let $\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}$ and $\{v_{m+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ denote bases for $V$ and
   624	  $W$, respectively.
   625	  Thus the set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$ forms a basis for $\F_{q^k}^n$, and from the
   626	  previous item, the set $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{i,\, j}$ is a basis for
   627	  $\F_q^{kn}$.
   628	  Furthermore, the sets $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\,i = 1,\ldots m}$ and
   629	  $\{ \downsize_q(e_j v_i) \}_{j,\, i = m+1,\ldots n}$ are bases for
   630	  $\downsize_q(V)$ and $\downsize_q(W)$, respectively.
   631	
   632	  There is a unique choice of coefficients $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that
   633	  $\downsize_q(z) = \sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j v_i)$.
   634	  But then
   635	  \begin{align*}
   636	    \downsize_q(z) & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl ( \sum_j
   637	                     \alpha_{i, j} e_j \bigr) v_i \Bigr) \\
   638	                   & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \alpha_i v_i \Bigr)\;,
   639	  \end{align*}
   640	  where we define $\alpha_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly
   643	  $z^W = \sum_{i=m+1}^n \alpha_i v_i$).
   644	  This implies that
   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}
   649	  and similarly $\downsize_q(z)^{W'} = \downsize_q(z^W)$.
   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,

   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational

    65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u

    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}

    75	    \begin{cases}

    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
